props.title: Japanese Girls Never Die

sections.content: **Japanese Girls Never Die (2016)** (2016) marks a striking entry in contemporary Japanese cinema's examination of gender dynamics and societal pressure. Director Daigo Matsui crafts a non-linear narrative that interweaves multiple storylines centered around the disappearance of office worker Haruko Azumi. The film shares thematic DNA with other provocative Japanese social commentaries like **Confessions** (2010) and **Love Exposure** (2008), particularly in its bold visual style and unflinching look at youth culture. Its street art narrative thread recalls **Banksy Does New York** (2014), but with a distinctly Japanese feminist perspective.

sections.content: The film's structural complexity mirrors works like **Happy Hour** (2015) and **Side Job** (2017) in its exploration of women's experiences in contemporary Japan. The spray-painted images of the missing Haruko becoming a viral phenomenon speaks to themes found in **Tag** (2015) and **Suicide Club** (2001) - how media and imagery can take on unintended meanings in modern Japanese society. The film's commentary on workplace harassment and gender inequality connects to earlier works like **Office** (2015) and **Harmonium** (2016). SUBHEAD: Visual Style and Social Commentary

Matsui's distinctive visual approach combines security camera footage, smartphone videos, and traditional cinematography to create a fractured narrative that reflects modern Japan's media landscape. This technique recalls experimental works like **Noriko's Dinner Table** (2005) while addressing contemporary issues of viral fame and social media influence. The film's pink-tinged color palette and urban nightscapes create a dreamlike atmosphere similar to **Tokyo Vampire Hotel** (2017), though deployed for more grounded social commentary.
